sentences.text: This dinosaur reached a length of about 4.8 meters and had a mass of 265 kilograms.
Other estimates suggest it measured roughly 4.5 meters long and weighed 250 kilograms.
It is known for possessing powerful forelimbs that exceeded 65 centimeters in length, a feature often reduced in related species.
The hand kept four metacarpals, and the shoulder blade showed a unique bump on the acromial region not seen in other meat-eaters.
Recent analysis shows its finger bones were short, resembling those of the ceratosaurian Saltriovenator.
Dong Zhiming gave the species the name Xuanhanosaurus qilixiaensis in 1984.
Fossil hunters recovered the remains in 1979 while surveying dinosaurs in Sichuan Province.
The main specimen, cataloged as IVPP V.6729, came from the Lower Shaximiao Formation.
This holotype includes parts of the shoulder, chest, front legs, and back spine, but lacks a skull.
Scientists believe the robust arms might have helped the animal catch its food.
Most experts classify it as a tetanuran, perhaps an early relative of allosauroids, noting the leftover fourth finger bone.
The original describer placed it in Megalosauridae and viewed it as a mid-level tetanuran because of the vestigial fourth metacarpal.
In 2009, Roger Benson determined it belonged to an ancient line of Megalosauroidea.
By 2018, arguments suggested it sat on early branches connecting ceratosaurs and tetanurans.
Later, Rauhut and Pol moved it outside Metriacanthosauridae to become the most basic member of Allosauroidea.
While Dong assigned it to Megalosauridae, other researchers like Holtz et al. see it as a non-coelurosaurian tetanuran.
The Paleobiology Database lists its parent group as Piatnitzkysauridae.
That same database records its family as Piatnitzkysauridae.
It inhabited the Sichuan Basin in China during the Middle Jurassic, specifically the Bathonian age, around 166 million years ago.
It also lived in what is now Asia during the Callovian stage of the Middle Jurassic, spanning from 167 to 161 million years ago.

There is disagreement over whether Xuanhanosaurus walked on four legs; the original author claimed it was the only known four-legged meat-eater, but later scientists argue it used only its hind legs because the arms could not rotate inward.
